Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-LXX). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. source_text: XXXIV. Igitur, ex mente Doctorum istorum, Gratia excitans consistit in mentis quadam illuminatione, & piis quibusdam cogitationibus, affectibus & desideriis, in hominum animis, non expectato illorum consensu, immediate a Deo excitatis. Ad quae proinde mens & voluntas hominis physice quidem concurrit, quoniam sunt actus vitales, a facultatibus illis profluentes, sed tamen non libere: quia sunt actus indeliberati, qui mentis consultationem, & electionem voluntatis praeveniunt.
english: Thesis XXXIV. On the view of these doctors, then, rousing grace consists in an enlightening of the mind and in devout thoughts, feelings and desires that God stirs up directly in human souls without waiting for their consent.

The human mind and will do take a physical part in these, since they are living acts that come from those faculties. But they do not take part freely, because these are undeliberate acts, which come before the mind has weighed anything and before the will has chosen.

source_text: XXXV. Gratia vero adjuvans, ex eorundem Doctorum sententia, praecipue consistit in dono & auxilio quodam ordinis supernaturalis, quo voluntas elevatur, & juvatur ad eliciendos actus, qui naturales ejus vires superant. Quod auxilium voluntatem movet physice atque effective: sed tamen non concurrit ad opus supernaturale prius natura, quam liberum arbitrium: neque se habet proprie, ut causa totalis, respectu actus supernaturalis, sed ut causa partialis duntaxat.
english: Thesis XXXV. Assisting grace, in the opinion of the same doctors, consists chiefly in a gift and help of the supernatural order by which the will is lifted up and helped to produce acts beyond its natural strength.

This help moves the will physically and effectively. Yet it does not concur in the supernatural work before free choice in the order of nature, and with regard to the supernatural act it is not, strictly, the total cause but only a partial one.

source_text: XXXVI. Qui autem distinctius enumerant ea in quibus gratia illa excitans consistit, ad eam referunt, primo internam quandam auditionem, & praeconceptionem veritatum fidei, quae assensum antecedit. Deinde coruscationes quasdam divinas, quibus ita derepente percellitur mens nostra, ut nova quadam & inusitata luce experiamur nos cognoscere & intueri magnitudinem & dignitatem rerum divinarum; aut etiam foeditatem peccatorum, & exiguitatem rerum humanarum, & alia ejusmodi, quae attentius animadversa, atque considerata, vehementer hominem movent, ut ad Deum se totum convertat.
english: Thesis XXXVI. Those who list more precisely what this rousing grace consists of include in it, first, an inner hearing and preliminary grasp of the truths of faith, which comes before assent.

Next they include certain divine flashes that strike our mind so suddenly that, in a new and unfamiliar light, we find ourselves knowing and seeing the greatness and worth of divine things, or else the foulness of sin, the smallness of human affairs and the like. When these are noticed and weighed with more attention, they move a person powerfully to turn wholly to God.

source_text: XXXVII. In hoc genere quoque ponunt interiorem quandam delectationem in voluntate, ex ejusmodi illustrationibus sequi solitam. Et praeterea varios motus qui divinitus excitantur in appetitu: qualia sunt amor, timor, spes, dolor, & confusio, & similes affectiones, quibus trahitur, & inclinatur interdum ratio superior, ut virtutem sectetur, & declinet vitia.
english: Thesis XXXVII. Under this heading they also place an inner delight in the will, which usually follows such enlightenments.

They add various movements that God stirs up in the appetite, such as love, fear, hope, sorrow, shame and similar feelings. By these the higher reason is sometimes drawn and inclined to pursue virtue and turn away from vice.

source_text: XXXVIII. Imo quanquam auxilium illud speciale, quod in excitans & adjuvans dividunt, in internis animi motibus, ut dictum est, proprie consistat; multi tamen ad gratiam excitantem revocant etiam externa quaedam: ut sunt occasiones & opportunitates, quas divina providentia suppeditat homini, ut in eo excitentur hujusmodi motus, tam in intellectu, quam in appetitu. Cujusmodi sunt infirmitas, pericula, boni socii, adversitates, & alii varii eventus: sicut videre est apud Gregorium de Valentia loco modo citato. Et similiter Alvares notat gratiam excitantem comprehendere excitationem, tum externam, quae fit per creaturas & signa sensibilia; tum etiam internam, quae fit a Deo immediate, quum immittit pias cogitationes, & proponit ea quae inducere possunt liberum arbitrium ad actum fidei & charitatis, & alias supernaturales operationes. De auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 8. disp. 75.
english: Thesis XXXVIII. Indeed, although that special help, which they divide into rousing and assisting, strictly consists in inward movements of the soul, as has been said, many also count certain outward things as rousing grace. These are the occasions and opportunities that God's providence supplies to a person so that such movements may be stirred in him, in both the intellect and the appetite.
Examples are sickness, dangers, good companions, misfortunes and various other events, as may be seen in Gregory of Valencia at the place just cited.

Alvarez likewise notes that rousing grace includes both an outward rousing, which comes through creatures and signs perceived by the senses, and an inward one, which comes directly from God when he puts devout thoughts into the mind and sets before it what can lead free choice to the act of faith and charity and to other supernatural works (De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 8, disputation 75).

source_text: XXXIX. Verum alii Scholae Romanae Theologi distinctionem gratiae in excitantem atque adjuvantem diverso plane modo exponunt atque intelligunt. Patet enim ex dictis, juxta priores illos, gratiam excitantem esse, per quam homo excitatur & sollicitatur ad bonum, licet illud nondum velit: adjuvantem autem esse, per quam homo adjuvatur ut velit, ac deinde faciat. Quo referunt illud Apocalypseos, Ecce ego sto ad ostium & pulso, si quis audierit vocem meam, & aperuerit mihi januam, intrabo ad illum, &c. Sed posteriores isti de quibus jam agimus, locum illum de gratia excitante non exponendum esse censent. Dicunt enim non esse idem pulsare & excitare. Quoniam multis adhibetur pulsatio, tum per externum ministerium praedicationis, exhortationis & increpationis, tum per internas illustrationes & inspirationes, qui tamen a somno peccati, vel negligentiae non excitantur, neque evigilant, sed consopiti manent, qui proinde nondum dici possunt excitantem gratiam habere. Quemadmodum & iis accidit, qui corporis somno detinentur, ut pulsatione adhibita, non tamen statim expergiscantur.
english: Thesis XXXIX. Other theologians of the Roman school, however, explain and understand the division of grace into rousing and assisting in quite another way. From what has been said it is clear that for the first group rousing grace is the grace by which a person is roused and urged toward good even though he does not yet will it, and assisting grace is the grace by which he is helped to will it and then to do it.
To this they apply the text of Revelation: 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I will come in to him,' and so on.

The second group, whom we are now discussing, holds that this text should not be taken of rousing grace, because knocking and rousing are not the same thing. Many people are knocked at, both through the outward ministry of preaching, exhortation and rebuke and through inward enlightenments and inspirations, and yet are not roused from the sleep of sin or neglect. They do not wake up but stay sound asleep, and so they cannot yet be said to have rousing grace.
It is the same with people held by bodily sleep: someone knocks, yet they do not wake at once.

source_text: XL. Igitur per gratiam excitantem intelligunt illam qua homini peccatori, aut a bono opere cessanti, & tanquam quodam sopore depresso, ita immittitur cogitatio, desiderium, & voluntas boni operis, ut jam vere excitatus a somno peccati, aut negligentiae bonorum operum dici possit. Gratiam vero adjuvantem vocant illam qua is qui jam est excitatus adjuvatur, ut perfectius velit quod jam velle incepit: utque perficiat quod jam voluit. Excitat enim, inquiunt, gratia ut velimus, adjuvat ut faciamus. Excitantis gratiae est velle; adjuvantis facere atque perficere. Quae interpretatio est Gulielmi Estii in lib. 2. sentent. distinct. 26. paragr. undecimo.
english: Thesis XL. By rousing grace, then, they mean the grace by which a sinner, or one who has stopped doing good and lies as if sunk in a kind of sleep, is given the thought, desire and will to do a good work, in such a way that he can now be said to be truly roused from the sleep of sin or from neglect of good works.
By assisting grace they mean the grace by which someone already roused is helped to will more perfectly what he has begun to will, and to carry out what he has already willed.

'Grace,' they say, 'rouses us to will and assists us to do. Willing belongs to rousing grace; doing and completing belong to assisting grace.' This is the interpretation of William Estius on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 11.

source_text: XLI. Eodem modo istam gratiae partitionem in excitantem atque adjuvantem explicat Jansenius Episcopus Iprensis, de gratia Christi salvatoris libro quarto capite decimo sexto. Quemadmodum, inquit, haec proprie vocatur Excitans, quae bonum voluntatis motum in potentia voluntatis excitat, ubi non erat nisi malus, vel quae excitat potentiam voluntatis mortuam sopitamque Deo, ut accepto bene volendi motu, incipiat vivere & vigilare; ita Adjuvans illa proprie ab Augustino & Patribus vocatur, quae jam excitato acceptoque bonae voluntatis motu, hominem jam volentem conantemque adjuvat, ut vel efficiat quod voluerit, vel ut fortius velit quod velle coepit, carnisque concupiscentiam acceptae voluntati pertinacissime resistentem superet. Quod ut clarius explicet, in praecedentibus docet, in ista divisione excitationem gratiae non tam esse quamlibet provocationem, vel incitationem ad actum, quam primam suscitationem, seu excitationem, sive emicationem sopitae, mortuae extinctaeque volitionis bonae.
english: Thesis XLI. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, explains this division of grace into rousing and assisting in the same way, in book 4, chapter 16 of his treatise on the grace of Christ the Saviour.

'Rousing grace,' he says, 'is properly the grace that stirs up a good movement in the will's power where there was only a bad one, or that wakes the will's power, which is dead and asleep toward God, so that once it has received the movement of willing well it may begin to live and stay awake.

In the same way Augustine and the Fathers properly give the name assisting grace to the grace that, once the movement of good will has been stirred and received, helps the man who already wills and strives, either to carry out what he has willed, or to will more strongly what he has begun to will, and to overcome the desire of the flesh that stubbornly resists the will he has received.'

To explain this more clearly, he teaches in the preceding pages that rousing, in this division, is not so much any urging or prompting to act as the first awakening, rousing or flaring up of a good volition that was asleep, dead and extinguished.

source_text: XLII. In Scholis quoque Romanis trita & celeberrima est gratiae divisio in Operantem, & Cooperantem. Quae sumpta est ex verbis Augustini, in libro de Gratia & libero Arbitrio capite decimo septimo. Ipse, inquit, ut velimus operatur incipiens, qui volentibus cooperatur perficiens. Et paulo post, ut velimus, inquit, sine nobis operatur. Quum autem volumus, & sic volumus, ut faciamus, nobiscum cooperatur. Adeoque juxta communem & confusam quandam notionem, Gratia Operans dicitur, quae sola sine nobis operatur. Cooperans vero, quae non operatur sine nobis, sed cui cooperamur.
english: Thesis XLII. In the Roman schools, too, the division of grace into operating and cooperating is familiar and very well known. It is drawn from Augustine's words in On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 17: 'He works at the start, so that we may will; and he cooperates with those who will, to bring the work to completion.' A little later he says: 'He works without us so that we may will; but when we will, and will in such a way that we act, he cooperates with us.'
So on a common and rather loose understanding, operating grace is the grace that works alone, without us, and cooperating grace is the grace that does not work without us but with which we cooperate.

source_text: XLIII. Sed non convenit inter Theologos Ecclesiae Romanae, quae sit illa gratia quae sine nobis operatur: & etiam quae sit illa quae nobis cooperatur, & quomodo, & quatenus illi cooperemur. Vetustiores Scholastici, testante Bellarmino, gratiam Operantem vocant ipsum habitum gratiae, ut formaliter nos justos & gratos Deo reddit, Id enim Deus in nobis, sine nobis facit. Gratiam cooperantem esse volunt eundem habitum, ut operis meritorii principium est. Quum enim bona opera facimus, non sola gratia operatur in nobis: sed & nos ipsi vere cooperamur.
english: Thesis XLIII. The theologians of the Roman Church, however, do not agree on which grace it is that works without us, or which grace cooperates with us, or how and how far we cooperate with it.

The older scholastics, according to Bellarmine, give the name operating grace to the habit of grace itself, insofar as it formally makes us righteous and pleasing to God, since God does this in us without us. They take cooperating grace to be the same habit insofar as it is the source of meritorious works: when we do good works, grace is not the only thing at work in us, but we ourselves also truly cooperate.

source_text: XLIV. Verum hodierni plerique Ecclesiae Romanae Doctores, per gratiam operantem intelligunt, eam per quam in nobis producuntur illi animi motus, qui sunt indeliberati, & a Libero consensu voluntatis nostrae non pendent. Quales sunt piae cogitationes, & mentis illustrationes, & etiam pia quaedam desideria, quibus a Deo movemur atque sollicitamur ad fidem & conversionem.
english: Thesis XLIV. Most present-day doctors of the Roman Church, however, take operating grace to mean the grace by which those movements of the soul are produced in us that are undeliberate and do not depend on our will's free consent.
These are devout thoughts, enlightenments of the mind and also certain devout desires, by which God moves and urges us toward faith and conversion.

source_text: XLV. Ac monent hanc gratiam recte dici in nobis, sine nobis operari, non quod mens & voluntas nostra mere passive se habeant ad motus illos quos in nobis producit: Cum enim sint motus vitales, a potentia vitali, inquiunt, efficienter procedere debent: sed quia per illam Deus in nobis operatur, sine nobis moraliter, seu libere concurrentibus; licet non sine nobis Physice operantibus. Non enim, ut aiunt, illae actiones nobis tribui solent, quae fiunt sine libertate, quaeque dicuntur actiones hominis; sed eae duntaxat ad quas nos libere determinamus, & quae proprie actiones humanae appellantur.
english: Thesis XLV. They point out that this grace is rightly said to work in us without us, not because our mind and will are merely passive toward the movements it produces in us, for since these are living movements they must, they say, come efficiently from a living power.
It is said so rather because by this grace God works in us without our concurring morally, that is, freely, though not without our acting physically.

For, as they say, the actions usually credited to us are not those that happen without freedom, which are called acts of a man, but only those to which we freely determine ourselves, which are properly called human acts.

source_text: XLVI. Consequenter autem per gratiam cooperantem intelligunt illam quae in nobis producit liberum illum voluntatis consensum, quo vocationi divinae obsequimur, aliosque deinceps voluntatis nostrae actus, quibus in bono pergimus, magisque ac magis ad Deum convertimur. Illam vero vocari dicunt non operantem, sed cooperantem, quoniam libere cum ea concurrimus; nec actus illi qui ei tribuuntur, a sola gratia procedunt, sed etiam a nostro libero Arbitrio.
english: Thesis XLVI. Accordingly, by cooperating grace they mean the grace that produces in us the free consent of the will by which we obey God's call, and the further acts of our will by which we keep on in good and turn more and more to God.
They say it is called cooperating rather than operating because we concur with it freely, and the acts credited to it come not from grace alone but also from our free choice.

source_text: XLVII. Itaque quod dicit Augustinus, gratiam sine nobis operari ut Velimus, intelligunt de actu voluntatis indeliberato, & de imperfecto quodam desiderio. Quod autem addit, Quum Volumus nobiscum cooperatur, intelligunt de actu voluntatis consummato, & de electione perfecta & deliberata. Et sic gratiam operantem & cooperantem exponunt communiter hodie Jesuitae, & plurimi Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, qui a partibus eorum stant contra Dominicanos & Thomistas recentiores. Ut videre est apud Becanum libello de Auxiliis Gratiae juxta Catholicos, qui liber est inter ejus opuscula. Et Petrum a sancto Joseph in Idea Theologiae speculativae, lib. 4. cap. 6. Resolutione 4.
english: Thesis XLVII. Augustine's statement that grace works without us so that we may will, they take to refer to the undeliberate act of the will, an imperfect sort of desire. His addition, that when we will he cooperates with us, they take to refer to the completed act of the will, a choice that is perfect and deliberate.

This is how the Jesuits commonly explain operating and cooperating grace today, together with very many doctors of the Roman Church who side with them against the Dominicans and the more recent Thomists.

This may be seen in Becanus's short treatise De auxiliis gratiae juxta Catholicos, which is among his minor works, and in Peter of Saint Joseph, Idea theologiae speculativae, book 4, chapter 6, resolution 4.

source_text: XLVIII. Quibus consentanea docet Gabriel Vasquez, nempe gratiam operantem esse ipsam sanctam cogitationem, quae est ante consensum, atque eodem modo motum voluntatis subitum, sine nostra libertate ex pia illa cogitatione ortum, quo deterremur a malo & ad bonum provocamur: gratiam vero cooperantem esse in consensu libero, in quo jam meritum aliquod reperitur, sive vitae aeternae condignum, sive impetratorium alicujus doni. Deum enim in nobis sine nobis operari sanctam cogitationem, & primum motum voluntatis non deliberatum, quae duo sunt initium bonae operationis & salutis nostrae: at consensum ipsum, quem huic vocationi praebemus, Deum operari nobiscum. in 1. Thom. to. 1. Disput. 88. cap. 6. num. 20.
english: Thesis XLVIII. Gabriel Vasquez teaches in agreement with them that operating grace is the holy thought itself, which comes before consent, and likewise the sudden movement of the will that arises from that devout thought without our freedom, by which we are held back from evil and urged toward good.
Cooperating grace, he says, lies in the free consent, in which some merit is already found, either merit that strictly deserves eternal life or merit that obtains some gift by asking.

For God works in us without us the holy thought and the first undeliberate movement of the will, which together are the beginning of good action and of our salvation; but the consent itself that we give to this call God works with us (on Thomas, part 1, tome 1, disputation 88, chapter 6, number 20).

source_text: XLIX. Caeterum Andreas Vega, inter Doctores illos qui Concilio Tridentino interfuerunt non parum celebris, eadem quidem, quae jam dicti Doctores, ad gratiam operantem refert, nempe sanctam cogitationem & primum motum voluntatis, quo homo subito movetur ad bonum. Sed censet alia de causa Deum dici ista in nobis sine nobis operari. Nimirum quia ad istius motus, & sanctae istius cogitationis productionem, Deus solus physice operatur, homo autem passive omnino se habet; In eo siquidem hominem non solum non agere libere, sed nequidem physice actionem ullam elicere. Quod autem istum Doctorem impulit ut ita sentiret, illud est, quod cum Scholasticis illis, qui Mominales appellantur, existimavit in homine a solo Deo efficiente posse produci intellectionem, & volitionem aliquam, intellectu & voluntate omnino patiente, nec agente ullo modo, etiamsi illa qualitate homo informatus intelligere & velle dicatur: quia licet ista grammatice ut actiones hominis exprimantur, non sunt tamen revera, in eo casu, actiones & productiones mentis & voluntatis, sed solum qualitates, quae suo effectu formali reddunt hominem intelligentem & volentem, qua de re videndus Vasquez disputationis modo citatae cap. 3.
english: Thesis XLIX. Andres de Vega, however, a man of no small note among the doctors who attended the Council of Trent, assigns to operating grace the same things as the doctors just named, namely the holy thought and the first movement of the will by which a person is suddenly moved toward good. But he holds that God is said to work these in us without us for a different reason.

His reason is that in producing that movement and that holy thought God alone acts physically, while the man is entirely passive: in it he not only does not act freely, but does not even produce any action physically.

What led this doctor to that view is that, with the scholastics called Nominalists, he thought that God, as sole efficient cause, could produce in a man an act of understanding or of willing while the intellect and will were wholly passive and did nothing at all, even though the man shaped by that quality is said to understand and to will.

Though these are expressed grammatically as a man's actions, in that case they are not really actions or products of the mind and will, but only qualities that by their formal effect make the man understanding and willing. On this see Vasquez, chapter 3 of the disputation just cited.

source_text: L. At vero sunt alii qui per gratiam operantem designari putant eam, quae efficit in homine primum actum deliberatae voluntatis: qualis est conversio, sive ab infidelitate ad fidem, sive a peccatis caeteris ad poenitentiam. Per gratiam vero cooperantem intelligunt illam quae efficit consequentes actus voluntatis: quales sunt velle orare, velle bona opera facere, & alii similes. Ita ut gratia operans nihil sit aliud quam auxilium speciale efficax respectu primi actus voluntatis: gratia vero cooperans sit auxilium speciale efficax quoque, respectu actuum sequentium.
english: Thesis L. Others, however, think that operating grace means the grace that produces in a person the first act of deliberate will, such as conversion, whether from unbelief to faith or from other sins to repentance.

By cooperating grace they mean the grace that produces the later acts of the will, such as willing to pray, willing to do good works and the like. On this view operating grace is simply special, efficacious help with regard to the will's first act, and cooperating grace is likewise special and efficacious help with regard to the acts that follow.

source_text: LI. Haec est sententia Bellarmini, qui pertendit merito posse dici Deum operari in nobis, sine nobis, primum illud Velle deliberatum, quo ad Deum convertimur: licet non tantum physice, sed etiam libere a voluntate nostra eliciatur. Nam, inquit, si consideremus causam efficientem illius actus, ea non solum est Deus per auxilium speciale; sed etiam voluntas per liberum arbitrium; & hoc modo Deus illum operatur non sine nobis. At si consideremus causam ejusdem actus moralem, id est, causam suadendo, hortando, consulendo, ea solus est Deus. Non enim ipsa se voluntas impellit suadendo, & hortando, ut velit quod non vult; sed Deus per inspirationes suas intus animae loquens, ei suadet, & persuadet ut velit. Igitur, juxta illum, gratia operans est, quae praevenit conatum & industriam nostram, & operatur ut velimus quod antea nolebamus, sine nobis operantibus ut velimus; non tamen sine nobis libere consentientibus, dum volumus.
english: Thesis LI. This is Bellarmine's view. He argues that God can rightly be said to work in us without us that first deliberate act of willing by which we turn to God, even though our will produces it freely and not merely physically.

'If we consider the efficient cause of this act,' he says, 'it is not only God through special help but also the will through free choice, and in this sense God does not work it without us. But if we consider its moral cause, that is, the cause that persuades, urges and advises, that cause is God alone.
For the will does not drive itself by persuading and urging itself to will what it does not will; it is God who, speaking inwardly to the soul by his inspirations, urges and persuades it to will.'

On his view, then, operating grace is the grace that comes before our effort and diligence and brings it about that we will what we did not will before. It does so without our working to make ourselves will, though not without our freely consenting when we will.

source_text: LII. Gratia autem illa quae requiritur ad reliquos actus voluntatis, post primum, ex ejus sententia, dicitur cooperans, quoniam postea quam coepimus converti ad Deum, jam nos ipsi non tantum per liberum arbitrium producimus, Deo juvante, reliquos actus; sed etiam nos incitamus & impellimus, Deo cooperante, ad eos. Itaque, inquit, gratia operans est quae facit nos velle credere; quia id in nobis fit, sine nobis petentibus, ac multo minus laborantibus & conantibus: Et gratia cooperans, quae facit nos velle orare, jejunare, & eleemosynas dare: quia id non fit nisi conatu, & industria nostra cooperante. Unde colligit Deum non operari velle nostrum sine nobis; sed tantum operari ut velimus sine nobis: quoniam scilicet, Deo cooperamur volendo, id est, libere producendo actum volendi; sed non cooperamur faciendo ut velimus. Quia non ipsi nos movemus & incitamus ad volendum: sed ipse solus interna inspiratione nos movet atque impellit.
english: Thesis LII. In his view the grace needed for the will's later acts, after the first, is called cooperating, because once we have begun to turn to God we not only produce the later acts through free choice with God's help, but also spur and drive ourselves to them, with God cooperating.

'So operating grace,' he says, 'is the grace that makes us will to believe, since this happens in us without our asking for it, much less toiling and striving for it; and cooperating grace is the grace that makes us will to pray, fast and give alms, since this does not happen except with our effort and diligence cooperating.'

From this he concludes that God does not work our willing without us, but only works without us the fact that we will. For we cooperate with God in willing, that is, in freely producing the act of willing, but we do not cooperate in bringing it about that we will, because we do not ourselves move and spur ourselves to will; he alone moves and drives us by an inward inspiration.

source_text: LIII. Eodem recidit quod docet Estius, Gratiam operantem vulgo dici in nobis sine nobis operari, quoniam primus conversionis actus, seu primus bonus voluntatis motus, qui ejus gratiae effectus est, a voluntate quidem est, tanquam a principio activo & libero; sed tamen Deus illum per gratiam suam operatur, sine praevio in nobis alio motu voluntatis, quo ad primum illum motum conemur, aut aspiremus, aut quo voluntas eum sibi imperet. Quippe cum interdum homini, etiam valde repugnanti, inspiretur bonus affectus voluntatis, ut in Paulo contigit. Cujus conversio, quantum attinet ad mutationem illam ex malo in bonum factam per gratiam operantem, forma est & exemplar conversionis omnium peccatorum. Quoniam per Dei gratiam ex aversis convertuntur & ex nolentibus volentes redduntur. Reliquos vero voluntatis actus, qui primum illum consequuntur, & quibus Deo pergimus adhaerere, gratia Dei quidem operatur quoq; in nobis; sed tamen voluntas nostra ad Deum jam conversa, non solum illos libere producit, verum etiam per alios anteriores actus sibi imperat. Et ita modo quodam singulari cooperatur divinae gratiae, quae propterea hoc respectu dicitur cooperans. In 2. Sentent. Dist. 26. §. 11.
english: Thesis LIII. Estius's teaching comes to the same. Operating grace, he says, is commonly said to work in us without us because the first act of conversion, the first good movement of the will, which is the effect of that grace, does indeed come from the will as from an active and free source. Yet God works it by his grace without any earlier movement of the will in us by which we strive or aspire toward that first movement, or by which the will commands it of itself.

Indeed a good disposition of the will is sometimes breathed into a person even while he strongly resists, as happened with Paul. His conversion, as regards that change from evil to good brought about by operating grace, is the pattern and model for the conversion of all sinners, since by God's grace they are turned from being averse and made willing from being unwilling.

The later acts of the will that follow that first one, by which we go on clinging to God, are also worked in us by God's grace. But our will, now turned to God, not only produces them freely but also commands them of itself through other earlier acts.
In this way it cooperates with divine grace in a special manner, and for this reason the grace is called cooperating in this respect (on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, section 11).

source_text: LIV. Non dissimili modo Gratiam operantem & cooperantem explicat Jansenius Episcopus Iprensis. Gratia, inquit, operans est illa quae sola sine studio, sine oratione, sine merito hominis praecedente, voluntatem, seu velle operatur, per quod voluntas ex mala fit bona, & ex injusta justa. Cooperans vero quae homini jam volenti, conantique cooperatur, firmam illam augendo roborandoque voluntatem, ut id efficiat & perficiat quod voluerit & conatur. Ibidemque ex Augustino docet gratiam operantem esse, qua cum ante nollemus, efficitur ut velimus: cooperantem, qua quando jam actu volumus, efficitur ut fortius velimus, ita ut superando quaevis obstacula, etiam reipsa faciamus. Illam operari ut quoquomodo voluntatem bonam, seu velle bonum habeamus: hanc ut illa bona voluntas augeatur & roboretur. Unde colligit cooperantem gratiam nunquam dici respectu primae voluntatis bonae, quando in eam erumpit potentia voluntatis, quoniam illa prima voluntas, seu volitio bona, est solius gratiae operantis effectus, sed solum respectu bonae voluntatis postquam homo jam velle coepit, ut illud velle perseveret, augeatur, bonisque operibus velut fructibus cumuletur.
english: Thesis LIV. Jansenius, bishop of Ypres, explains operating and cooperating grace in much the same way. 'Operating grace,' he says, 'is the grace that by itself, with no prior effort, prayer or merit on man's part, works the will, or the willing, by which the will is made good from bad and just from unjust.

Cooperating grace is the grace that cooperates with a man who already wills and strives, by enlarging that will and strengthening it to firmness, so that he may accomplish and complete what he has willed and is striving for.'

In the same place he teaches from Augustine that operating grace is the grace by which, when we did not will before, we are brought to will; and cooperating grace the grace by which, when we already actually will, we are brought to will more strongly, so that by overcoming every obstacle we also actually do it. The first works so that we have a good will, a willing of good, in some way or other; the second, so that this good will may be enlarged and strengthened.

From this he concludes that cooperating grace is never spoken of with respect to the first good will, when the will's power breaks out into it, since that first will, or good volition, is the effect of operating grace alone. It is spoken of only with respect to good will after a person has begun to will, so that this willing may last, grow and be enriched with good works as with fruit.

source_text: LV. Gratia operans igitur, ut diligenter observat, sola primam bonam voluntatem in homine efficit, non quod homo non simul in illam voluntatem, hoc est, in voluntatis motum atque consensionem influat, sed quia motum illum gratia operatur, nobis nihil ad eum habendum conferentibus, petendo, desiderando, studendo, meditando, atque ita nihil omnino boni meriti, respectu illius voluntatis, afferendo. Illud enim impossibile esse, hoc ipso quo statuitur, esse prima voluntas bona, ad quam ex mala convertitur. Vicissim vero gratia cooperans sic dicta est, quia operatur aliquid in nobis non sola, sed nobis simul cooperantibus; non per simultaneum tantum influxum, quo etiam cooperamur gratiae operanti, sed praevie ad effectum istius gratiae, Volendo, credendo, desiderando, petendo, pulsando, satagendo, adeoque etiam promerendo; ita ut ejus gratiae cooperantis effectus sit universum primae voluntatis illius bonae incrementum, usque ad apicem perfectionis humanae. De gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 4. cap. 15.
english: Thesis LV. Operating grace, then, as he carefully observes, alone produces the first good will in a person. This is not because the person does not at the same time contribute his own influence to that will, that is, to the will's movement and consent, but because grace works that movement while we contribute nothing toward having it, whether by asking, desiring, striving or meditating, and so bring no good merit whatever with respect to that will.
Such merit is impossible, he says, for the very reason that this is laid down to be the first good will, to which one turns from a bad will.

Cooperating grace, in turn, is so called because it works something in us not alone but with us cooperating at the same time. It does so not merely by a simultaneous influence, by which we cooperate with operating grace too, but ahead of that grace's effect, by willing, believing, desiring, asking, knocking, taking pains and so even meriting.
Thus the effect of cooperating grace is the whole growth of that first good will, up to the height of human perfection (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 4, chapter 15).

source_text: LVI. Ab his omnibus differt sententia Didaci Alvares. Existimat enim ille ad quamcunque piam operationem, sive sit interior, sive sit exterior; sive sit prima illa qua ad Deum convertimur, sive quaelibet alia eam sequens, semper concurrere gratiam operantem, & gratiam cooperantem. Et quidem gratiam operantem esse, per quam Deus Physice praedeterminat voluntatem nostram ad consensum in quodvis bonum opus: cooperantem vero, per quam Deus quamlibet actionem piam nobiscum operatur. Utrumque enim necessarium esse, & ut Deus praemoveat liberum nostrum arbitrium Physice & efficienter ad quemvis actum supernaturalem; & ut concurrat cum eodem libero arbitrio, quod jam a Deo praemotum se movet ad bonum opus. Gratiam autem operantem dici in ordine ad primum effectum, respectu cujus voluntas nostra solum se habet, ut mota: cooperantem vero, in ordine ad secundum, in quo mota se movet. Idque quoniam voluntas nostra in ordine ad motionem praeviam, qua movetur a Deo ad actus supernaturales, habet se passive, cum talis motio non producatur active a nostro libero arbitrio, sed solum a Deo, a quo est auxilium illud operantis gratiae. Et rursus voluntas mota a Deo producit active & libere operationes supernaturales, cum gratia Dei concurrente. Ac proinde gratia Dei, priore illo respectu, operatur sine nobis: posteriore vero illi cooperamur. De Auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 9. Disp. 81.
english: Thesis LVI. Diego Alvarez's view differs from all of these. He holds that in every devout work, whether inward or outward, whether it is the first by which we turn to God or any later one, operating and cooperating grace always both take part.

Operating grace is the grace by which God physically predetermines our will to consent to any good work; cooperating grace is the grace by which God works any devout action together with us. Both are needed: God must premove our free choice physically and efficiently to any supernatural act, and he must also act together with that same free choice, which, once premoved by God, moves itself to the good work.

Grace is called operating with regard to the first effect, in relation to which our will is only moved; and cooperating with regard to the second, in which the will, having been moved, moves itself. This is because our will is passive toward the prior motion by which God moves it to supernatural acts, since that motion is produced not actively by our free choice but by God alone, from whom that help of operating grace comes.

The will, moved by God, then actively and freely produces supernatural works, with God's grace acting together with it. So in the first respect God's grace works without us, and in the second we cooperate with it (De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 9, disputation 81).

source_text: LVII. Hic autem quaerunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, quomodo Gratia operans distinguatur ab excitante: & gratia cooperans a gratia adjuvante. Sed ex jam dictis facile colligi potest quid ad hanc quaestionem, juxta uniuscujusque placita, respondendum sit. Etenim illi qui, cum Vasquezio, Molina, & plerisque Jesuitis, per gratiam excitantem intelligunt tantum gratiam Pulsantem & Sollicitantem, & quidem saepe frustra: per gratiam vero Adjuvantem, illam qua Deus concurrit auxilio speciali cum libero arbitrio, dum gratiae consentit, & ei obsequitur: Ac rursus per gratiam operantem, illam quae in nobis efficit pias cogitationes, & motus indeliberatos, ad quos Physice quidem, sed non libere concurrimus; per cooperantem vero, illam quae in nobis producit liberos voluntatis actus, quibus Deo vocanti & invitanti respondemus; illi, inquam, existimant gratiam operantem eandem esse cum excitante, & gratiam adjuvantem eandem cum cooperante. Nempe juxta illos, eadem gratia, & dicitur excitans, quatenus per sanctas cogitationes, & desideria pia nobis immissa nos sollicitat & excitat ad bonum; Et operans, quatenus ista in nobis operatur, sine nobis libere concurrentibus, & consentientibus. Et similiter eadem gratia & adjuvans dicitur, quatenus nos adjuvat, dum invitanti gratiae consentimus; Et cooperans, quatenus non operatur sine nobis libere nostrum consensum praebentibus.
english: Thesis LVII. Here the doctors of the Roman Church raise the question how operating grace differs from rousing grace, and cooperating grace from assisting grace. From what has been said it is easy to work out how each party must answer, according to its own positions.

Some, with Vasquez, Molina and most of the Jesuits, take rousing grace to mean only the grace that knocks and urges, and that indeed often in vain; assisting grace, the grace by which God concurs by special help with free choice while free choice consents to grace and obeys it; operating grace, the grace that produces in us devout thoughts and undeliberate movements, in which we take part physically but not freely; and cooperating grace, the grace that produces in us the free acts of the will by which we answer God when he calls and invites.

These people hold that operating grace is the same as rousing grace, and assisting grace the same as cooperating grace. For them one and the same grace is called rousing insofar as it urges and rouses us to good through the holy thoughts and devout desires it puts into us, and operating insofar as it works these in us without our freely concurring and consenting.

Likewise one and the same grace is called assisting insofar as it helps us while we consent to grace's invitation, and cooperating insofar as it does not work without us, as we freely give our consent.

source_text: LVIII. Eodem modo gratia excitans eadem est cum operante, & gratia adjuvans eadem cum cooperante, omnibus illis, qui cum Jansenio & Estio per gratiam excitantem intelligunt illam, quae revera excitat peccatorem a somno peccati, & per adjuvantem illam qua homo adjuvatur, ut perficiat bonum quod jam velle incepit: Ac per operantem eam quae in nobis efficit primum conversionis actum, per cooperantem eam quae alios sequentes, ad quos non tantum libero quodam voluntatis influxu, sed etiam praevio aliquo studio & conatu nostro cooperamur.
english: Thesis LVIII. Rousing grace is likewise the same as operating grace, and assisting grace the same as cooperating grace, for all who, with Jansenius and Estius, take rousing grace to be the grace that actually wakes the sinner from the sleep of sin, and assisting grace the grace by which a person is helped to complete the good he has already begun to will.

They also take operating grace to be the grace that produces in us the first act of conversion, and cooperating grace the grace that produces the acts that follow, in which we cooperate not only by a free contribution of the will but also by some prior effort and striving of our own.

source_text: LIX. Sed qui, cum Jansenio & Estio, volunt quidem gratiam operantem dici, quae in nobis operatur primam conversionem; & cooperantem, quae nos movet ad bona opera quae inde consequuntur: sed pertendunt cum Jesuitis gratiam excitantem esse, qua pulsamur ut a somno vitiorum evigilemus, etiamsi culpa nostra sopiti saepe maneamus; adjuvantem vero quae nos roborat & adjuvat, dum somnum istum revera excutimus: illi, inquam, ut Bellarminus, gratiam excitantem ab operante distinguunt, & consequenter gratiam adjuvantem a cooperante: Nam illis gratia excitans latius patet quam operans. Adeoque gratiam excitantem dividunt in sufficientem atque efficacem. Et rursus efficacem in operantem & cooperantem, ut videre est apud eundem Bellarminum libro 1. de Gratia saepius jam citato.
english: Thesis LIX. Others agree with Jansenius and Estius that operating grace is the grace that works the first conversion in us, and cooperating grace the grace that moves us to the good works that follow from it.

But they maintain with the Jesuits that rousing grace is the grace by which we are knocked at so that we may wake from the sleep of vice, even if through our own fault we often stay asleep, and assisting grace the grace that strengthens and helps us while we actually shake off that sleep.

These, like Bellarmine, distinguish rousing grace from operating grace, and so assisting grace from cooperating grace, since for them rousing grace covers more ground than operating grace. They therefore divide rousing grace into sufficient and efficacious, and efficacious grace again into operating and cooperating, as may be seen in Bellarmine, book 1 On Grace, already cited many times.

source_text: LX. Similiter Alvares gratiam excitantem distinguit ab operante: quoniam gratia excitans ipsi est gratia quaedam voluntatem ad bonum moraliter tantum trahens & alliciens. Operans vero, gratia non solum moraliter, sed etiam physice voluntatem ad bonum praemovens & praedeterminans. Adeoque, juxta ipsum, gratia excitans eadem est cum gratia sufficiente. Gratia vero operans & cooperans pertinent ad gratiam efficacem.
english: Thesis LX. Alvarez likewise distinguishes rousing grace from operating grace. For him rousing grace is a grace that draws and attracts the will toward good only morally, while operating grace not only morally but also physically premoves and predetermines the will toward good.
So on his view rousing grace is the same as sufficient grace, whereas operating and cooperating grace belong to efficacious grace.

source_text: LXI. Sed inter Scholae Romanae Theologos praecipua hic controversia est de modo quo Der gratia cum voluntate nostra cooperatur. Etenim Jesuitae, & alii complures Scholae Romanae Doctores, negant gratiam adjuvantem, sive cooperantem prius natura concurrere ad opus supernaturale, quam liberum arbitrium; Et hoc ne admittant, gratiam praedeterminare liberum arbitrium. Unde, ipsorum judicio, periret libertas voluntatis; cui, ex ista hypothesi, gratia divina imponeret aliquam agendi necessitatem, quae cum libertate consistere non posset. Sic inter alios sentit & ratiocinatur Petrus a sancto Joseph, in idea Theologiae speculativae, libro quarto, capite sexto, ubi sic incipit ejus tertia Resolutio, Gratia adjuvans uon concurrit prius natura ad opus supernaturale, quam liberum arbitrium.
english: Thesis LXI. Among the theologians of the Roman school, however, the main dispute here concerns the way in which God's grace cooperates with our will.

The Jesuits and many other doctors of the Roman school deny that assisting or cooperating grace concurs in the supernatural work before free choice in the order of nature. They do so in order not to admit that grace predetermines free choice, since in their judgment the freedom of the will would then perish: on that supposition divine grace would lay on the will some necessity of acting that could not stand with freedom.

Peter of Saint Joseph, among others, thinks and argues this way in his Idea theologiae speculativae, book 4, chapter 6, where his third resolution begins: 'Assisting grace does not concur in the supernatural work before free choice in the order of nature.'

source_text: LXII. Contra vero pertendunt alii gratiam adjuvantem atque cooperantem, secundum causalitatis ordinem, praevenire liberum arbitrium, & prius quam illud agere: Ac quanquam simul tempore tam gratia, quam liberum arbitrium influant in piam operationem, natura tamen quodammodo priorem esse gratiae influxum, nec ordine causalitatis cum influxu liberi arbitrii simultaneum. Haec est sententia Didaci Alvares in Epitome de Auxiliis divinae gratiae, libro tertio, capite decimo nono, cujus hoc lemma est, Quod Gratia cooperans, in quantum cooperans, sit praeveniens, seu praemovens liberum arbitrium ad consensum, & non solum pariter, & simultanee cum illo in piam operationem influens. Idem vero caput his verbis incipit, Ex praemissis constat, quod gratia cooperans, quatenus ab excitante distinguitur, sit praeveniens liberam cooperationem arbitrii creati, non quidem prioritate temporis, sed rationis duntaxat & causalitatis.
english: Thesis LXII. Others, on the contrary, maintain that assisting and cooperating grace comes before free choice in the order of causality and acts before it does. Although grace and free choice act on the devout work at the same time, the influence of grace is in some way prior in nature, and is not simultaneous with the influence of free choice in the order of causality.

This is the view of Diego Alvarez in the Epitome of his work on the helps of divine grace, book 3, chapter 19, whose heading is: 'That cooperating grace, as cooperating, is prevenient, or premoves free choice to consent, and does not merely act on the devout work equally and simultaneously with it.'

The chapter itself begins: 'From what has been laid down it is clear that cooperating grace, insofar as it is distinguished from rousing grace, goes before the free cooperation of created choice, not by priority in time but only in reason and causality.'

source_text: LXIII. Neque propterea quicquam praejudicari putant libertati voluntatis humanae; quoniam gratia Dei sic movet & determinat liberum arbitrium creatum ad agendum, ut ab eo non tollat potestatem aliter agendi: ita ut posita gratia, agat quidem infallibiliter, sed semper in sensu diviso potens sit non agere, aut aliter agere.
english: Thesis LXIII. They do not think this harms the freedom of the human will in any way. God's grace moves and determines created free choice to act in such a way that it does not remove its power to act otherwise.
So when grace is given, the will does act without fail, yet in the divided sense it always remains able not to act or to act otherwise.

source_text: LXIV. Praeterea qui Molinae Jesuitae Methodum & doctrinam sequuntur, docent gratiam adjuvantem, sive cooperantem non se habere proprie ut causam totalem, respectu actus supernaturalis, sed ut causam partialem duntaxat. Et hoc quia gratia adjuvans, ex eorum sententia, non producit actum supernaturalem, nisi dependenter a Libero arbitrio.
english: Thesis LXIV. Further, those who follow the method and teaching of the Jesuit Molina hold that assisting or cooperating grace is not, strictly, the total cause of the supernatural act, but only a partial cause.
Their reason is that, in their view, assisting grace produces the supernatural act only in dependence on free choice.

source_text: LXV. Admittunt quidem totum actum supernaturalem a gratia pendere: verum addunt illum non pendere ab ea totaliter, sed partialiter tantum: quia gratia, scilicet, nequit illum producere, nisi dependenter a concursu voluntatis. Ac proinde gratiam posse quidem dici causam totalem actus boni totalitate effectus, sed non totalitate causae, de qua hic agitur: quoniam totus quidem effectus a gratia pendet, sed tamen ut a causa quae illum non producit sine alia causa concurrente, & simul cum ea agente. Unde est quod comparant gratiam & liberum arbitrium duobus equis currum eundem simul trahentibus, quorum neuter altero prius agit, & alterum movet ad agendum, & qui tractionis illius sunt causae tantum partiales; licet tota tractio dici possit, ab equis singulis dependere, quia singuli ad totam tractionem aliquid conferunt.
english: Thesis LXV. They grant that the whole supernatural act depends on grace, but add that it depends on grace not totally but only in part, because grace cannot produce it except in dependence on the will's concurrence.

Grace can therefore be called the total cause of the good act by totality of effect, but not by totality of cause, which is the point at issue here. The whole effect does depend on grace, but as on a cause that does not produce it without another cause acting with it at the same time.

That is why they compare grace and free choice to two horses pulling the same cart together. Neither of them acts first and moves the other to act, and each is only a partial cause of the pulling, although the whole pulling can be said to depend on each horse, since each contributes something to all of it.

source_text: LXVI. Itaque ex eorum mente, gratia adjuvans ut sic & praecise considerata, non movet hominem ad agendum, sed illum juvat in actuali operatione. Gratia excitans vero, etsi hominem moveat ad agendum, non tamen illi imponit agendi necessitatem; sed illi suas partes relinquit, ut se nimirum determinet ad opus pium, cum alioqui possit ab eo abstinere, si velit, & aliter se determinare. Unde nec illa dici debet causa totalis, sive adaequata bonae operationis, ut videre est apud eundem Petrum a sancto Joseph loco supra citato.
english: Thesis LXVI. On their view, then, assisting grace taken strictly and as such does not move a person to act, but helps him in the actual working.

Rousing grace, though it does move a person to act, does not lay on him any necessity of acting. It leaves him his own part to play, namely to determine himself to the devout work, since otherwise he can refrain from it, if he wishes, and determine himself differently.
So it too should not be called the total or adequate cause of the good work, as may be seen in the same Peter of Saint Joseph at the place cited above.

source_text: LXVII. Contra vero Estius & Thomistae recentiores docent gratiam Dei ita esse totalem causam boni operis, ut quicquid est in opere boni totum faciat, & totum opus sit gratiae divinae ascribendum, tanquam causae totali, non solum tanquam partiali.
english: Thesis LXVII. Estius and the more recent Thomists, by contrast, hold that God's grace is the total cause of a good work in such a way that it produces all the good there is in the work. The whole work must therefore be credited to divine grace as its total cause, and not merely as a partial one.

source_text: LXVIII. Sed quamvis absolute & proprie loquendo, asserant totum bonum opus esse a gratia Dei, nihilominus docent idem bonum opus totum esse a libero etiam arbitrio. Quia nihil prohibet aliquid totum esse a duabus causis, quarum una sit alteri subordinata: sic nimirum ut inferior causa omnem suam operandi virtutem, omnemq; motum accipiat a superiore. Atque hoc docent perpetuum esse in causa prima, & causa secunda; qualiscunque demum sit causa secunda, sive libere agat, sive naturaliter, quia, scilicet, necessarium est, ut quicquid fit a causa secunda referatur ad primam: Nec ullo modo potest in his admitti partitio operum: ut aliquid ulla sui parte existimetur fieri a causa secunda, quod non etiam totum, & omni parte fiat a causa prima applicante causam secundam ad omnem suam operationem.
english: Thesis LXVIII. Yet although, speaking absolutely and strictly, they assert that the whole good work comes from God's grace, they also teach that the same good work comes wholly from free choice as well.
Nothing prevents a thing from coming wholly from two causes when one is subordinate to the other, that is, when the lower cause receives all its power to act and all its motion from the higher.

This, they teach, always holds between the first cause and a second cause, whatever kind of second cause it may be and whether it acts freely or by nature, because whatever a second cause does must be traced back to the first.

Between these causes no division of the work can be admitted in any way, as if some part of it were thought to be done by the second cause that is not also done wholly, in every part, by the first cause, which applies the second cause to all its working.

source_text: LXIX. Dicunt igitur totum bonum simul & individuo opere peragi a gratia & libero arbitrio: nec esse distinctum quod est ex libero arbitrio, & quod est ex gratia; quia non est distinctum quod est ex causa prima, & quod est ex causa secunda. Sed inter utrumque agens docent illud esse discrimen, quod liberum arbitrium, sicut suum esse habet a Deo, ita & totum hoc quod bene operatur habet a gratia Dei, in ipso, & per ipsum operantis: non autem contra, vel in totum, vel ex parte, Deus in eo quod operatur, dependet a libero hominis arbitrio. Facit enim Deus ut homo faciat, non autem facit homo ut Deus faciat. Quae eadem ratio est in omni opere, seu actione, quae fit a quacunque causa secunda. Adeoque juxta hos Doctores, gratia divina, & liberum arbitrium non cooperantur ut causae partiales, quae in agendo pendeant ab invicem, sed ut causae totales atque subordinatae, quarum inferior pendet & movetur a superiore, non contra. Ut latius videre est apud eundem Estium in 2. sentent. distinct. 26. paragr. 29.
english: Thesis LXIX. They therefore say that the whole good is carried out by grace and free choice together, in one undivided work. What comes from free choice is not distinct from what comes from grace, just as what comes from the first cause is not distinct from what comes from the second.

Between the two agents, they teach, the difference is this: as free choice has its being from God, so it has all its good working from God's grace, which works in it and through it; but God, in what he works, does not in turn depend on man's free choice, either wholly or in part. For God causes man to act; man does not cause God to act.
The same holds in every work or action done by any second cause whatever.

So on the view of these doctors divine grace and free choice do not cooperate as partial causes that depend on each other in acting, but as total causes ordered one under the other, the lower depending on the higher and moved by it, not the reverse. This may be seen at more length in the same Estius on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 29.

source_text: LXX. Porro cum jam allatis gratiae divisionibus coincidunt aliae quaedam, quae parum aut nihil ab iis differunt. Ut quum gratia dividitur in gratiam praevenientem & in gratiam subsequentem: & in ducentem atque comitantem. Nam per gratiam ducentem atque praevenientem Theologi intelligunt illam eandem quam excitantem & operantem vocant: & per gratiam comitantem sive subsequentem, illam quae alias dicitur adjuvans, sive cooperans. Etenim illa gratia quae nos ad bonum excitat, & eatenus in nobis sine nobis operatur, eadem nos quoque praevenit: quae vero nos adjuvat in actuali operatione, nobisque cooperatur, eadem voluntates nostras in bene agendo censetur comitari, & priorem illam gratiam subsequitur. Nonnulli tamen quaedam subtilia discrimina inter hasce gratiae divisiones quaerunt, sed quae referre & commemorare non multum facit ad nostrum institutum. Quod potissimum hic considerandum restat, est celebris illa gratiae divisio in sufficientem atque efficacem: sed quia accurata ejus expositio res est longioris disquisitionis, in proximam disputationem illam differre visum est.
english: Thesis LXX. Some other divisions of grace coincide with those already given and differ little or not at all from them, as when grace is divided into prevenient and subsequent, and into leading and accompanying.

By leading and prevenient grace the theologians mean the same grace they call rousing and operating, and by accompanying or subsequent grace the grace otherwise called assisting or cooperating. The grace that rouses us to good, and to that extent works in us without us, also goes before us; the grace that helps us in the actual working and cooperates with us is held to accompany our wills in doing good, and comes after that first grace.
Some, however, look for certain subtle distinctions among these divisions of grace, but recounting and mentioning them would not do much for our purpose.

What chiefly remains to be considered here is the well-known division of grace into sufficient and efficacious. But since a careful account of it calls for a longer inquiry, it has seemed best to put it off to the next disputation.
